title: LiC14: “Are We Measuring ‘Bad Employees’ or Broken Climates? Rethinking Engagement in Context”
author: Leadership, Rewritten
summary: Writing as Leadership, Rewritten, Richard Claydon asks what employee engagement surveys actually measure and argues that engagement is too often treated as a moral score on employees rather than a signal about the climates leaders and systems create. Using a fictional character, Maya, as a through-line, he compares Kahn's self-in-role view, the Utrecht work engagement scale and Gallup-style consultancy models, then reads them through Lewin's idea that behaviour is a function of person and environment. He traces how quantified climate drifts into character judgment, notes the WEIRD bias in positive-psychology engagement constructs, and names the power choice behind who gets to interpret scores. His practical shifts are to read climates rather than fix people, to treat engagement as ongoing inquiry rather than an annual ritual, and to tell honest stories about what low scores imply for leaders.
points: Engagement is a moment-to-moment negotiation between self and role shaped by meaningfulness, safety and availability.
Survey scores are rough climate sensors, and treating them as verdicts on people hides leadership and design choices.
A single engagement number is politically convenient because it keeps leaders' styles and structures off the diagnostic map.
Leaders should ask what kind of field would make a low score a rational response before asking how to raise it.
Honest use of engagement data means accepting that some answers will implicate the leaders who designed the climate.
quotes: For Kahn, engagement isn’t a trait (“I am an engaged person”) or even a stable state (“I am highly engaged in this job”). It’s a moment-to-moment, context-dependent negotiation between self and role.

The problem isn’t the tools themselves. It’s what happens when we forget which lens they came from—and start using them to blame the person in the survey, rather than the system that made ticking “strongly disagree” feel like the only honest option.

Lewin’s point wasn’t that one group of boys was “naturally disengaged” and another “just more committed.” It was that style in context produced climates, and climates produced behaviour. Change the style or the structure, and the “same” people behave differently.
The climate (E) quietly disappears from the story. All that’s left is the “engaged” or “disengaged” person (P) – as if they turned up that way from home.

I/O psychologists are increasingly saying, “We need systems thinking.” Many HR leaders say, “We know engagement is about environment, not just attitude.” Yet the tools and narratives still drag us back toward WEIRD individualism.
The problem isn’t that we measure engagement. It’s what we quietly decide those measurements are about.
